summary:
Mizoram stands under India's national framework, which applies directly to the state: Parliament's Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, passed in March 2026, replaces the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Presidential assent remained pending as of late March 2026.

Human Rights Watch reported on 26 March 2026 that the amendment reverses the 2014 Supreme Court ruling and requires medical certification for identity recognition. It adds offences carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring anyone to be transgender, which Human Rights Watch warns could criminalise support networks. The BBC reported the same day that medical boards and district authorities must now certify gender-affirming surgery.

Recognition is thin in practice: of 487,803 census-recorded transgender persons, only about 32,500 hold identity cards. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The government presents the narrower definition as targeting welfare benefits and anti-trafficking protection. Critics warn it excludes many trans men, trans women and non-binary people, and a Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel asked the government to withdraw the bill, calling removal of self-identification a setback against the 2014 ruling. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

For a visitor, exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone: recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, and abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters was documented in 2024 and 2026, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people.
tangentialFactors:
The amendment's status is unsettled. Presidential assent was still pending in late March 2026, and a Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel had asked the government to withdraw the bill, so the operative text at any given moment may differ from the version passed by Parliament.

The two principal accounts of March 2026 describe the recognition test in different terms. Human Rights Watch frames it as recognition restricted to traditionally recognised groups and intersex persons; the BBC reports recognition based on biological or physical traits alongside traditional identities. Both agree that self-identification has been removed and that medical certification now governs recognition.

The gap between legal recognition and administrative uptake is wide. Fewer than one in fourteen census-recorded transgender persons hold an identity card, which suggests that document friction at checkpoints is likely to arise from incomplete paperwork as much as from hostile officials.

Human Rights Watch's warning that the new coercing-or-alluring offence could criminalise support networks places peer groups, activists and service providers in an adjacent risk category to the visitor, since contact with community organisations may itself attract scrutiny under the amended text.

The direction of legislative and judicial movement runs opposite ways. Parliament narrowed recognition in March 2026 while the Madras High Court issued binding-style guidelines on police conduct and conversion therapy in 2021, and the Allahabad High Court ordered relief over passport medical screening in February 2026.
localsOnly:
Identity recognition now runs through medical boards and district authorities, which certify gender-affirming surgery before an identity document is issued. Residents seeking or renewing documents face this certification route rather than a declaration of self-identified gender.

Welfare scheme eligibility and anti-trafficking protection are the government's stated grounds for the narrower definition, so access to state benefits is tied to falling within a traditionally recognised group or the intersex category.

The amendment creates a criminal offence, punishable with up to life imprisonment, for coercing or alluring anyone to be transgender. Community organisers, counsellors and family members who assist someone in transitioning may fall within its reach, according to Human Rights Watch.

Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, in force since 2024, the gender-identity-specific offences of the former Indian Penal Code no longer apply. Trans communities report fear of a rise in sexual assaults without those provisions, and there is no replacement safeguard identified in the sources.

Police sensitisation obligations, the ban on conversion therapy and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities derive from the Madras High Court's 2021 judgment in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police. These are court-issued guidelines of one state's high court rather than nationwide statutory duties, and their application outside that jurisdiction is not established in the sources.

Only about 32,500 of the 487,803 census-recorded transgender persons hold identity cards, so most residents seeking to use identity documents for services will encounter the certification process for the first time.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Mizoram-specific source appears in the inventory. State-level police practice in Mizoram, local facilities, state NGOs, and any Mizoram legislation or government orders on transgender persons are not sourced here and remain unresolved.

Whether presidential assent was subsequently given, and whether the amendment has been notified and brought into force, is unresolved as of the latest source date of 26 March 2026.

The inventory does not state whether Mizoram has its own transgender recognition or welfare procedure distinct from the national process, or whether district authorities in the state apply the certification route described nationally.

The two March 2026 accounts differ on how the recognition test is worded, one emphasising traditionally recognised groups and intersex persons, the other biological or physical traits plus traditional identities. The exact statutory wording is not sourced.

Whether the Madras High Court's 2021 guidelines and the February 2026 Allahabad High Court relief have any binding effect in Mizoram is not sourced.

The December 2025 UK Home Office country note is a foreign government assessment and covers India as a whole; its findings for Mizoram specifically are not broken out in the inventory.
